uncited: **Determine the bounding box:** Identify the integer coordinates $(i, j, k)$ such that $i \le x < i+1$, $j \le y < j+1$, and $k \le z < k+1$.
**Identify neighbor indices:** In 3D, cubic interpolation requires 4 points along each axis.
The indices for the x-axis are $i-1, i, i+1, i+2$.
Similarly for y ($j-1, j, j+1, j+2$) and z ($k-1, k, k+1, k+2$).
**Apply 1D Cubic Kernel:** For each dimension, apply a cubic filter kernel $K(u)$ to the 4 sampled values.
The general form of the cubic kernel depends on parameters $B$ and $C$ (see [Cubic Interpolation (Mitchell-Netravali)](2073-cubic-interpolation-mitchell-netravali.md)).
**Tensor Product:** The final 3D value is the tensor product of the 1D interpolations along each axis.
- Boundary handling: Clamping, wrapping, or reflection.
- **Boundary conditions:** Accessing indices $i-1$ or $i+2$ may go out of bounds.
**Pitfall:** High computational cost: On-the-fly tri-cubic filtering is costly.
This is a root-finding problem for a cubic polynomial, solved using the cubic formula.
Cubic interpolation in volume rendering originated as a higher-order alternative to linear methods to improve visual smoothness.
